items.author: konard
items.body:
This issue can be done as alternative to https://github.com/deep-foundation/dev/issues/125, but in this case it will allow to use any IDE with SyncTextFile links.

For SyncTextFile we can use Supports links to determine which file extension should be for that file.
The name of the file should be defined via Contain link's value.

For AsyncFile we can use files table with metadata to determine the file extension.
The name of the file should be defined via Contain link's value.

Users, Spaces, Packages should be interpreted as folders.

At the moment if the name of file is not defined in the Contain link's value, then this link is not exported as file. When we create supported file in the file system SyncTextFile/AsyncFile with appropriate name in Contain link should be created.

This should be done as CLI that can synchronize on demand or on changes in files.

This feature can be also used to synchronize multiple folders for example iCloud, Google Drive, Dropbox and so on.

https://habr.com/ru/articles/777252/#comment_26211370 - additional info about the problem.

items.title: Files support for packager
items.author: konard
items.body:
There should be away to export binary files to deep.json or a folder near it.

This should be a universal solution that will work with all package managers and all programming languages. NPM, NuGet and so on.

At the moment, the best guess is to use `base64` as the value of `AsyncFile` links.

Later, we can support paths relative to `deep.json` or `deep.xml` instead of `base64` in `value` filed of the link. It should start with `.` to distinguish it from `base64`, for example `./assets/6F9619FF-8B86-D011-B42D-00CF4FC964FF.jpg`. `6F9619FF-8B86-D011-B42D-00CF4FC964FF` is an GUID of `AsyncFile` link (it may be extracted from files table or just regenerated on the fly). The extension `.jpg` and so on can be extract from the name of the file in `files` table or from the meme type. GUID is best to ensure `AsyncFile` with the same upload names will not overlap in `assets` folder.

`assets` folder itself is not mandatory, but optional, and it can be chosen by the user of `Packager` class.

We should start the MVP from only `base64` support, if this becomes a problem we can add support for relative paths, or may be even `https` links to static file storage on the internet.

_Note that NPM may not like that packages are used as file store._

items.title: Dynamic PostgreSQL indexes
items.author: konard
items.body:
1. Create all indexes for all columns in the table: https://gist.github.com/Konard/8d2866bcc55192aa24c887b40553419d
2. Collect indexes usage statistics
3. Collect statistics about executed queries
4. Translate statistics from 2 and 3 steps into sequences of columns that are used and their usage frequency (https://github.com/Konard/LinksPlatform/issues/589 can be related)
5. Once in the moment of time, use N most frequent sequences of columns as combined indexes, all other combined indexes that are not in whitelist are deleted. 

This way we get dynamic adaptation of indexes to queries and indexes usage statistics.

There should be setting that is updatable by user for changing the number of indexes used versus write speed and storage space used.

This way the user will be able to adjust what is more important to have good write speed or to have good read speed.

# Преимущества Теории Графов

1. Визуализация: Графы позволяют визуализировать сложные структуры и процессы, что облегчает их понимание и анализ.

2. Моделирование: Графы можно использовать для моделирования и анализа разнообразных ситуаций, от социальных сетей и веб-сайтов до транспортных маршрутов и сетей питания.

3. Использование алгоритмов: Теория графов предлагает большой набор алгоритмов для решения разнообразных задач, таких как поиск кратчайшего пути, поиск максимального потока и определение связности графа.

4. Допускают применение теории вероятностей: Это позволяет моделировать вероятностные процессы и события, такие как распространение болезней или слухов.

5. Масштабируемость: Графы поддерживают большие наборы данных, что делает их мощным инструментом для анализа и интерпретации больших данных.

6. Возможность представления сложных связей: Графы могут представлять сложные или нелинейные связи между объектами, что сложно сделать с помощью других структур данных.

7. Теория графов способствует точности представления данных: В отличие от некоторых других методов, она обеспечивает точное представление структурированных данных.

8. Междисциплинарность: Теория графов может быть применена в различных областях, включая компьютерные науки, математику, биологию, социологию и многое другое.

9. Роль в машинном обучении: Графы играют важную роль в некоторых алгоритмах машинного обучения, особенно в областях, таких как поиск в сети, распознавание образов и анализ социальных сетей.


# Преимущества Теории Связей

Вот и к этим преимуществам добавляется возможность представления строгих последовательностей и деревьев выражений, а так же AST и прочих подобных структур данных в ассоциативности. И автоматически единое адресное пространство, позволяющее связывать любые сущности с любыми сущностями.

Представление строгих последовательностей позволяет представлять весь спектр форм данных, и уже того что они могут представлять ленту машины тьюринга достаточно, чтобы ассоциативность могла описывать абсолютно любую структуру данных как есть с минимальным количеством искажений. До той степени, что структура может стать синонимом сети связи, чем она уже по определению и является.

Ассоциативность это самая очевидная идея, которую почему-то не осмелились сделать раньше. Которая обеспечивает максимальную возможную гибкость, адаптивность, принятие всех форм информации, и простоту.

Ассоциативность это так же именно то как большинство людей (вероятно даже все) мыслят. Причём ассоциативность может описывать как железо человека - то есть его нейросеть, так и эффекты логических ассоциаций, которые появляются только в софте этой нейросети.

Учитывая стремление к простоте в ассоциативности она позволяет находить более короткие пути решения тех или иных проблем.

Ассоциативность требует меньше сущностей чем теория графов.

А значит в некоторых случаях может занимать и меньше места, а следовательно вычисляться быстрее, так как меньше данных будет необходимо подгружать.

Минимально одну связь можно представить 1 битом в матрице.

Чтобы поддержать рекурсивность, нужно как минимум 2 бита, то есть по одному биту в двух матрицах, или 1 битом в 3-х мерной или 4-х мерной матрице.

Ассоциативная теория в отличие от теории графов - рекурсивна.

А значит позволяет рекурсивно определять концепции, причём в отложенном стиле.

И из этих базовых преимуществ может следовать целый спектр выводимых преимуществ число которых бесконечность.

И это только на основе `@deep-foundation/core` пакета.

Это не все пакеты, которые идут с Дипом из коробки.

items.title: The doublets store is opened, rebuilt and dropped on every access: hold one instance for the process lifetime behind an RwLock
items.author: konard
items.body:
`associative::write_binary` and `read_binary` each open the file, memory-map it and construct a fresh `unit::Store` on **every** call, then drop it. Nothing survives between calls, so the token store pays a full open-map-build-teardown cycle per access — and on the write path, a complete reconstruction of the semantic graph.

This is what makes a read-only `list()` take 8–14 seconds while the underlying disk write is 0.25 s (measurements in #356). `doublets` is not slow. It is being opened, rebuilt and thrown away thousands of times over.

## What happens today

Write (`storage/associative.rs:300`):

```rust
let file = options.create_new(true).open(&tmp)?;        // a NEW file every time
let mapped = LoadedFileMapped::new(file)?;               // a NEW 64 MB mapping
let mut store = unit::Store::<usize, _>::new(mapped)?;   // a NEW store
write_semantic_links(&mut store, records)?;              // rebuild the ENTIRE graph
drop(store);                                             // and throw it away
… sync_all, rename, sync_directory
```

Read (`storage/associative.rs:343`) does the same minus the rebuild:

```rust
let file = OpenOptions::new().read(true).write(true).open(path)?;
let mapped = LoadedFileMapped::new(file)?;
let store = unit::Store::<usize, _>::new(mapped)?;
let links = read_semantic_links(&store)?;
```

And `write_semantic_links` re-interns every string and re-creates every link for every record, including records that did not change. With 306 tokens that is on the order of 8,000 `intern_string` and 8,000 `create_link` calls to persist a change to one token — or, via the unconditional `commit()` in `with_records`, to answer a request that changed nothing at all.

## The store is meant to be long-lived

A `doublets` store backed by a file is designed to be opened once and used for the life of the process. The crate already exposes everything needed to mutate it in place — `create`, `update`, `update_by`, `delete_by`, `each_by` (`doublets-0.4.0/src/data/traits.rs`) — none of which this crate calls. Only `create_link` is used, and only against a store that was just built empty.

Opening once and keeping the handle also makes the 64 MB mapping a one-time cost at startup instead of a per-request one, and removes the `create_new` + `rename` dance from the hot path entirely.

## What this issue asks for

**Hold one `Store` instance for the process lifetime and guard it with a read-write lock.**

`BinaryTokenStore` is already shaped for this — it holds `Arc<RwLock<…>>` today, just with a `HashMap` inside it instead of the store:

```rust
pub struct BinaryTokenStore {
    path: PathBuf,
    lock_path: PathBuf,
    inner: Arc<RwLock<HashMap<String, TokenRecord>>>,   // <- the store belongs here
}
```

Concretely:

1. **Open once** in `BinaryTokenStore::open` and keep the `Store` in `inner`.
2. **Reads take the read guard** and query the live store — no file open, no mapping, no reconstruction. Concurrent reads proceed in parallel.
3. **Writes take the write guard** and apply an incremental change — `update`/`delete_by`/`create` for the affected record only, not a rebuild of all 306.
4. **Keep the cross-process `flock`** where it is still needed. The in-process `RwLock` protects the shared handle; the file lock protects against a second router process on the same data directory. They answer different questions and both have a place — but a shared (`lock_shared`) file lock is enough for readers, which is available on the same primitive already in use.

Related and best sequenced together: #356 (the unconditional `commit()` on the read path — that fix alone stops reads from touching the store) and #351.

## Suggested tests

- a `list()` performs no file open and no mapping after the first (assert via an instrumented count, or simply that mtime and open-count do not change);
- writing one token does not re-create links belonging to other tokens;
- N concurrent readers do not serialise;
- a reader in flight does not block on a writer holding only the in-process lock when the data is unchanged;
- a second process opening the same directory still observes the cross-process lock;
- reopening after a crash mid-write recovers the last committed state.

## Note

Reported alongside #356, which measured where the time goes. This issue is the structural answer to it: the cost is not the storage engine, it is discarding and rebuilding it on every access.

items.title: Store all router state as links notation: the token store already does, the request log and three smaller stores still use JSON
items.author: konard
items.body:
## Summary

The token store already persists as links notation — `tokens.lino` alongside a `tokens.bin` backing store. Everything else the router persists still uses JSON: the request log as JSONL, the admin claim, the managed-server state, the server selection.

Requested: make links notation the storage format for **all** router-owned state, in a human-readable form, per the [associative tech stack](https://github.com/link-assistant/formal-ai/blob/main/docs/associative-tech-stack.md).

## Current state, from a live deployment

```
data/
  tokens.lino               6 KB     ← links notation
  tokens.bin               64 MB     ← binary link store
  tokens.lock, tokens.transaction.lock
  requests/<token-hash>/requests.jsonl   × 8   ← JSON Lines, 122 MB total
```

## What still uses JSON

| what | where | format |
|---|---|---|
| request log | `src/request_log.rs:166` → `requests/<hash>/requests.jsonl` | JSON Lines |
| admin claim | `src/admin.rs:52` → `admin-claim.json` | JSON |
| managed-server state | `src/managed_server_state.rs:52` → `managed-server.json` | JSON |
| server selection | `managed_server.rs` → `server.json` | JSON |

The request log is the bulk of it — 122 MB across eight token directories, versus 6 KB of links notation.

## The existing `.lino` file is not readable either

`tokens.lino` is stored base64-encoded on a single line:

```
(object ((str dHlwZQ==) (str Um91dGVyU3RhdGU=)) ((str c3VidHlwZQ==) (str VG9rZW5TdG9yZQ==)) …
```

(`dHlwZQ==` → `type`, `Um91dGVyU3RhdGU=` → `RouterState`, and so on.)

The cause is not in the router: `encode_text` (`src/storage/associative.rs:44`) calls `lino_objects_codec::encode`, which base64-encodes unconditionally. Filed upstream as [link-foundation/lino-objects-codec#37](https://github.com/link-foundation/lino-objects-codec/issues/37).

This matters here because moving the request log without that fix would produce 122 MB of single-line base64 — a formally associative store that is completely unusable for the analysis it is meant to enable (#234).

## Target format

One construct — `( )` — for both objects and arrays, at every level including the root. Indentation is for readability; content distinguishes the two: `key value` pairs make an object, bare values make an array.

```
(
  type "RouterState"
  server (
    host "127.0.0.1"
    port 18878
  )
  models (
    "claude-haiku"
    "claude-opus"
  )
  value (
    (
      id "7cf7abf6"
      label "bootstrap-admin"
      ttl_hours 24
      revoked false
    )
    (
      id "94b36f7e"
      label "wrapper-run"
      ttl_hours 720
      revoked false
    )
  )
)
```

| JSON | Links Notation |
|---|---|
| object, including the root | `( )` containing `key value` pairs, one per line |
| array | `( )` containing values, one per line |
| object as an array element | its own `( )` |
| string | double quotes, no encoding |
| number, `true`/`false`, `null` | bare, so the type survives the round trip |

This relies on parentheses opening a nested indentation context, released in `links-notation` **0.14.0** ([#283](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/pull/283)). Verified against that parser.

### Dependency upgrade this blocks on

`Cargo.toml` currently pins both crates to versions that predate the readable form:

```toml
lino-objects-codec = "0.2.1"
links-notation = "0.13.0"
```

Neither can produce the format above:

- `links-notation` 0.13 ignores indentation inside `( )`, so every line collapses into one flat list — record boundaries are lost;
- `lino-objects-codec` 0.2.1 base64-encodes every string and emits one line, regardless of the parser underneath.

So this issue depends on [link-foundation/lino-objects-codec#37](https://github.com/link-foundation/lino-objects-codec/issues/37) shipping a release whose default output is the readable form. **When that release exists, raise `lino-objects-codec` here to that version** (and `links-notation` to 0.14 or later, whichever the codec requires), then confirm the emitted files are readable.

Until then the remaining work — moving the request log and the three small stores — can proceed against the current codec, but the resulting files will not be readable, and the readability tests below will fail by design. Ordering the dependency upgrade first avoids writing a large store twice.

## Why the request log is the interesting case

It is where the associative model earns its keep rather than just satisfying a rule. A request log is naturally a link graph: an exchange links to its token, its surface, its model, its phases; a phase links to its body. Expressed that way, the questions in #234 — which streams ended without a terminator, which token produced repeated 401s, which exchanges have no terminal record — become traversals rather than substring searches over 100 MB of text.

Two defects found on this deployment came directly from JSONL's flatness:

- bodies are stored as UTF-8-mangled bytes when the upstream compresses (#231), because the record is a string field rather than an addressable value;
- a truncated stream is indistinguishable from a complete one (#230), because no link expresses "this exchange terminated, and how".

## What is being asked

1. Persist the request log as links notation with a binary link store, the same pairing already used for tokens — the volume warrants the binary side.
2. Move the remaining small state files (`admin-claim.json`, `managed-server.json`, `server.json`) to `.lino`. These are tiny and need no binary backing.
3. Raise `lino-objects-codec` to the release that makes the readable form its default (see **Dependency upgrade this blocks on**), so the router inherits it rather than reimplementing it.
4. State the rule in the docs: router-owned state is stored as links notation, and no other format is introduced.
5. Provide a migration path: read the old JSON/JSONL if present, write links notation from then on, and say so once in the log rather than failing.

## Scope boundary

The rule is about what the **router** stores. It does not extend to:

- files owned by client CLIs, which must keep whatever format that vendor reads;
- the HTTP wire format, dictated by the vendor APIs;
- `--json` output of CLI commands, which is a machine-readable interface, not storage.

## Tests worth adding

- every file the router creates under `DATA_DIR` parses as links notation;
- a file written by the router contains its keys (`type`, `subtype`, `value`) as visible text — no base64;
- `tokens.lino` written by the current build is readable, which is the signal that the dependency upgrade actually took effect;
- a deployment with pre-existing JSON state is migrated on first start, and the old files are left intact until the migration is confirmed;
- the request log round-trips: a recorded exchange read back yields the same phases, bodies and statuses;
- a body that is not valid UTF-8 survives the round trip (the failure mode behind #231);
- client configuration files are untouched by any of this.

## Note

Filed after inventorying a live deployment on router v0.93.0. The token store is already correct in mechanism; this is about the other four stores and about the readability of what all of them produce.

items.title: Storage does not use the associative stack: no doublets, and tokens.lino is hand-built string concatenation
items.author: konard
items.body:
## Requirement

Per the [associative technology stack](https://github.com/link-assistant/formal-ai/blob/main/docs/associative-tech-stack.md), persistent data should live in the associative store — links notation plus binary doublets — rather than in ad-hoc formats. Configuration should come through `lino-arguments` by default.

Current state on `main`: **configuration already complies; storage does not.**

## What already complies

`lino-arguments` is a direct dependency (`Cargo.toml:44`) and is the real configuration boundary:

```rust
// src/main.rs:45
let cli = <Cli as lino_arguments::Parser>::parse();
```

`src/cli.rs:28` uses `lino_arguments::Parser` as the clap-compatible drop-in. This matches the stack's description of `lino-arguments` as "the configuration boundary for the executable". No change needed here.

## What does not comply

### 1. No associative store at all

None of the storage components are dependencies. `grep -inE 'doublets|links-notation|platform-mem|lino-objects-codec' Cargo.toml` matches nothing (only `lino-arguments` is present).

The stack specifies `doublets-rs` backed by `platform-mem` as the native link-store backend, with Links Notation as the reviewable import/export projection. The router has neither: it defines its own dual store (`StoragePolicy::Both`) over two hand-rolled formats.

### 2. `tokens.lino` is not Links Notation — it is hand-built string concatenation

`encode_lino` (`src/storage.rs:497-520`) appends characters directly:

```rust
out.push_str("# Link.Assistant.Router token store\n");
out.push_str("# Format: (token <id> (label \"...\") ...)\n");
for rec in records {
    out.push('(');
    out.push_str("token ");
    out.push_str(&rec.id);
    out.push_str(" (label ");
    write_quoted(&mut out, &rec.label);
    …
```

No Links Notation parser or codec is involved in either direction. The `.lino` extension claims a format the file does not actually implement, so nothing guarantees it stays parseable by real Links Notation tooling — the shape is maintained by hand, and drift is invisible until an external tool tries to read it.

### 3. `tokens.bin` is a bespoke container around JSON

`src/storage.rs:285-302` defines a custom magic header (`LARTOK01`), and each record inside is `serde_json` (`:328`, `:412`). That is not the binary doublet representation the stack calls for — it is a private framing format that only this codebase understands.

### 4. Everything else is JSON

Beyond tokens, all persistent state uses JSON or JSONL: `credentials.json` and `auth.json` (`src/accounts.rs:569,852`; `src/auth.rs:545`), `audit.jsonl` (`src/audit.rs:190`), `requests.jsonl` (`src/logging.rs:13`), plus the client config files the router writes.

Some of these are **not** free to change — `credentials.json` and the client `settings.json` files must keep the exact shape their vendor CLIs expect, and those are interop boundaries rather than the router's own storage. That distinction should be drawn explicitly in the issue: convert the router's own state, keep foreign formats where a third party defines them.

## Suggested scope

1. Adopt `doublets` + `platform-mem` as the physical store for the router's own persistent state (tokens first — they are the core record, and the existing dual-store code is already isolated behind `TokenStore`).
2. Use the real `links-notation` parser and `lino-objects-codec` for the `.lino` projection instead of manual string building, so the exported form is genuinely parseable by the ecosystem's tools.
3. Reduce records to a link shape (the stack describes `Type → SubType → Value`) rather than serialising a Rust struct wholesale.
4. Decide per file whether it is router state (convert) or an interop boundary owned by a vendor (leave as is), and record that decision in the docs.
5. Migration path for deployments holding existing `tokens.lino`/`tokens.bin` files — reading the old formats must keep working, or an explicit conversion step must exist.

## Related

Fixing this also removes the root cause of the concurrent-write corruption filed separately: the dual hand-rolled store is what needed two writers racing over one temp path in the first place. Worth sequencing after that fix lands, so the two changes do not collide.

## Tests worth adding

- the router's own persistent state round-trips through the doublet store with no bespoke container format;
- the `.lino` projection is produced and consumed by the real Links Notation codec, and a file written by the router parses with the upstream parser (not just with this codebase's reader);
- reducing a record to links and reconstructing it is lossless;
- existing `tokens.lino`/`tokens.bin` files from an earlier version still load after the change;
- files owned by vendor CLIs keep their exact expected shape, asserted against the format those CLIs document.

After the persistent binary-store backend changed, a token store written by an earlier release could still be read but failed on every subsequent write. The issue path logged a warning while still returning a token, leaving the caller with a credential that was never persisted.

## Requirements

- Migrate a supported legacy binary store before accepting writes, or fail startup clearly.
- Never print or return a token unless persistence succeeds.
- Treat an unwritable token store as an error, not a warning.
- Preserve the readable text projection during migration.

## Regression coverage

Build a synthetic previous-version store, upgrade it, issue a token, and verify that the returned token appears in a subsequent list. A forced persistence failure must return non-zero and print no credential.

items.title: Token store capacity panics the issuing request after persisting an uncertain token
items.author: konard
items.body:
## Problem

A long-lived Router token store eventually reaches the fixed doublets mapping capacity. The next client-token issuance panics its Tokio worker and closes the HTTP connection without a response.

Verified independently on Router v1.4.6 and v1.5.0 with the same existing store:

```text
POST /api/management/tokens/client
curl: (52) Empty reply from server

thread tokio-rt-worker panicked at
doublets-0.5.0/src/mem/unit/generic/sources_recursionless_size_balanced_tree.rs:231:19:
index out of bounds: the len is 1049246 but the index is 1049246
```

The affected store had a 67,151,744-byte `tokens.bin` and a 13,980-line text projection. `tokens.bin` mtime advanced during the failed request, so the caller receives an uncertain result: it cannot know whether the returned credential was persisted because no credential or error response arrives.

This is reachable through ordinary use because `router with` and remote client setup mint tokens over time. It blocks a safe deployment that must issue and verify client-bound tokens before cutover. The existing Router process keeps running because only the request worker panics.

This is distinct from #356/#357 performance and #374 migration compatibility: the current format remains readable, but an in-place write reaches capacity and panics the request.

## Expected behavior

- Token issuance never panics at storage capacity.
- Router either grows/compacts the store and returns the persisted token, or returns a structured non-2xx error before exposing any credential.
- Expired and revoked ephemeral tokens do not grow the store without a practical bound.
- A failed write leaves the previous valid store intact and no ambiguous temporary file/result.
- Startup or health reports an actionable storage-capacity condition before issuance becomes unusable when recovery cannot be automatic.

## Regression coverage

- Build a synthetic token store immediately below capacity and issue one more client-bound token through the real HTTP route.
- Assert that the handler does not panic or close the connection.
- On success, the returned token is present after reopening the store.
- On forced capacity failure, the response is structured and non-2xx, no token is emitted, and the previous store reopens unchanged.
- Repeated `router with` token creation plus expiry/revocation stays bounded or is compacted before capacity is exhausted.

items.title: Stage 3: add crash-consistent writable filesystem
items.author: konard
items.body:
## Summary

- add a writable sector-device contract, writable loopback storage, deterministic power-loss injection, and VirtIO block write/flush requests
- add `Create`, `Write`, and `Sync` filesystem operations with `WRITE` capabilities and revoke-safe service behavior
- introduce format version 2 with a typed, bounded three-bank journal and two-flush generation commits
- replay the newest valid generation on mount and fall back to the previous checkpoint when the newest log is incomplete
- exercise durable create/write/sync/remount in the kernel and QEMU smoke path

## Crash consistency

A transaction copies the active log into the inactive target bank and appends its records. `Sync` then performs:

1. log writes
2. device flush
3. alternate superblock write with `generation + 1` and the log CRC
4. device flush

The active and previous banks remain untouched while a third bank receives the new transaction. This lets mount select the newest superblock whose journal validates, without fsck. The exhaustive fault test cuts power before every sector write and flush in a create/write/sync transaction and accepts only the complete old or new generation.

The journal is also the allocation policy for this bounded stage: object IDs are monotonic and the fixed banks have explicit capacity, so a separate free-space/object bitmap would duplicate state without enabling reuse. Exhaustion returns `FsError::Full`.

Format version 2 is intentionally incompatible with version 1 because the superblock now carries journal bank geometry and integrity metadata.

## Reproduction and tests

Before this change, block devices exposed reads only and `FsOp` had no create/write/sync variants, so a writable filesystem client did not compile. The new regression tests cover the missing API and behavior, including:

- writable and read-only loopback devices
- volatile writes, flush durability, and injected power loss
- typed log encoding and bounds
- create/write/sync/remount
- sparse/overlaid writes
- corrupted-newest-log fallback
- every power-cut checkpoint action
- write rights and stale capabilities after revoke
- the `MOLT_FS_WRITE_OK` kernel smoke marker

Local checks:

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --exclude molt-kernel -- -D warnings`
- `cargo clippy --package molt-kernel --target x86_64-unknown-none -- -D warnings`
- `cargo clippy --package molt-kernel --target riscv64gc-unknown-none-elf -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test --workspace`
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --exclude molt-kernel --no-deps`
- `cargo bench --package molt-core --no-run`
- `LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS=2 RUSTFLAGS="--cfg loom" cargo test --package molt-core --profile loom --lib`
- `cargo image`

Fixes #41

items.title: pngfs: mountable encrypted filesystem hidden in PNG and JPEG (Rust + WASM)
items.author: konard
items.body:
## pngfs — an encrypted, deniable filesystem you can **mount, edit and re-save** inside a picture

Closes #1.

A Rust core compiled to WebAssembly that hides an encrypted, deniable virtual
filesystem inside ordinary images — **PNG and JPEG** — plus a CLI and a 100 %
client-side web app (deployable to GitHub Pages). No servers, no uploads.

### Answering the latest review

> CTF generator — самый дешёвый вирусный канал, всё ещё свободен
> JPEG-robust mode (F5/JSteg) — мессенджеры по-прежнему убивают LSB при рекомпрессии - надо реализовать и доказать что всё работает
> Learn-вкладка (интерактивная стеганография)

| # | Point | What landed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **CTF generator** | `pngfs ctf -o challenge/` writes a **four-stage** capture-the-flag: a plain volume → a **deniable** one behind a decoy password → an **album** that rebuilds from 3 of its 4 pictures with a **Shamir**-split key → a **JPEG that has really been forwarded** through a re-compression. Covers are painted procedurally (`--covers` takes your own photos, `--seed` makes it reproducible), a `README.md` for players and an optional `SOLUTION.md` are written alongside. [`ctf::generate`](crates/pngfs-core/src/ctf.rs) **solves the whole chain against the bytes it is about to write** and returns an error rather than an unsolvable puzzle. |
| 2 | **JPEG-robust mode, proven** | Two JPEG modes over real DCT coefficients: **compact** (JSteg/F5, ±1 on nonzero AC) for capacity, and **robust** (QIM lattice, 3 copies per bit, heavy Reed–Solomon) for survival. The proof is a program, not a claim: `cargo run --release -p pngfs-core --example jpeg_robustness` re-encodes the stego picture with the **`image` crate's own encoder — code that knows nothing about pngfs** — and reads it back. Robust survives **q95 → q30**; compact is lost at the first re-encode, and the example says so. Same trip on the command line: `pngfs forward send.jpg --quality 60`. |
| 3 | **Learn tab** | A fifth tab in the web app: three lessons, every picture painted in the browser and every verdict computed by the same Rust core. See below. |

### The Learn tab

[![learn](https://github.com/uselessgoddess/pngfs-priv/blob/issue-1-7a3daf6d3d2a/docs/screenshots/learn.png?raw=true)](https://github.com/uselessgoddess/pngfs-priv/blob/issue-1-7a3daf6d3d2a/docs/screenshots/learn.png?raw=true)

Nothing on the tab is a mock-up or a pre-rendered asset — the covers are painted
by the page, the embedding is the WASM core, and the numbers come out of
`pngfs-core`'s own detectors.

1. **A bit in a pixel.** Type a sentence, watch it go in. The corner is magnified
   before and after (indistinguishable), both **last-bit planes** are drawn (noise
   before, noise after), the first ten carrier samples are printed in binary with
   the payload bit each one carries, and the container's **first bytes are
   reassembled from those very bits** — LSB-first over R, G, B with alpha skipped,
   exactly the order `pngfs_core::stego` writes them in.
2. **Why *matching*, not replacement.** The same bits are written into the same
   samples two ways — LSB *replacement* (the naive method, the only thing on the
   page written in JavaScript, because pngfs refuses to use it) and pngfs's ±1
   **LSB matching** — and both are judged by the chi-square detector in
   `pngfs-core`. A fill slider goes from 10 % to 100 %; replacement is flagged at
   every step (`p = 1.000` at 60 %, `p = 0.635` at 10 %), matching stays at the
   cover's baseline (`0.374` vs the untouched cover's `0.251`), and a **real pngfs
   volume filled to the brim** sits beside them at `0.192`. The pairs-of-values
   histograms underneath show *why*: the pairs level off under replacement and stay
   as uneven as the cover's under matching.
3. **What a messenger destroys.** The note is embedded twice — compact and robust —
   both pictures go through `jpeg::recompress` at a quality you choose, and both are
   read back **with no hint about how they were written** (the reader probes). At
   q75 and at q95 alike: compact → `destroyed ✗ — authentication failed`, robust →
   `survived ✓ — "the meeting is at nine"`.

`forward` is now exported from `pngfs-wasm`, so the browser runs the exact round
trip `pngfs forward` runs on the command line.

### Everything asked for in the issue

| Item | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Payload compression | ✅ brotli before encryption, kept only when it shrinks (this crate's source: **26.5 %**) |
| Read-write (edit in browser → re-save) | ✅ `Mount & edit`, only the unlocked slot is rewritten (1 612 of 2 880 000 samples on a 408 B save) |
| Folder drag & drop, progress bars, `pngfs list` | ✅ |
| Reed–Solomon / ECC | ✅ `--ecc standard\|heavy`, plus parity that always protects the 120-byte critical header |
| **JPEG support** | ✅ compact **and** robust, over real DCT coefficients |
| Multi-image sharding | ✅ CLI **and** the browser's `Album & shares` tab, erasure-coded |
| Shamir threshold passwords | ✅ `pngfs key`, GF(2⁸) — every unlock field in the web app also takes shares |
| Matrix (F5-like) encoding | ✅ `--coding matrix` (k=3) and `matrix4` |
| **CTF generator** | ✅ `pngfs ctf`, four stages, self-solving |
| **Learn tab** | ✅ three runnable lessons |
| Histogram-aware scatter | ⚪ deliberately not done — the container fills the *entire* capacity with payload-or-random by design (that is what makes an empty slot deniable), so every eligible sample is written whatever order they are chosen in |
| WebAuthn / YubiKey | ❌ not done |

### Honest caveats
- Robust JPEG mode buys survival with capacity — **1 130 B on a 640×480 cover**
  against compact's 15 KiB — and with a louder picture (31 dB against the cover,
  versus 52 dB for PNG LSB). It is for the kilobyte that has to arrive, not for
  the archive, and the Learn tab prints both numbers side by side rather than
  hiding the trade.
- Filling the whole capacity is what makes an empty slot deniable, and it means
  ~50 % of the low bits move on every PNG embed. Cheap for chi-square and RS (both
  stay at the cover's baseline, PSNR 52 dB), but a calibrated detector holding the
  original cover is a different game. Stated in the README's threat model.

### Screenshots
| Hide — capacity, tuning, self-test, pixel diff | Mount & edit — read-write in the browser |
| --- | --- |
| ![hide](https://github.com/uselessgoddess/pngfs-priv/blob/issue-1-7a3daf6d3d2a/docs/screenshots/hide.png?raw=true) | ![mount](https://github.com/uselessgoddess/pngfs-priv/blob/issue-1-7a3daf6d3d2a/docs/screenshots/mount.png?raw=true) |

| Album & shares — spread one volume over several pictures, split its key |
| --- |
| ![album](https://github.com/uselessgoddess/pngfs-priv/blob/issue-1-7a3daf6d3d2a/docs/screenshots/album.png?raw=true) |

### Verification
- `cargo test --workspace` — **107 tests + 7 doctests pass** (core 95, CLI 12),
  incl. dual-volume deniability, wrong-password rejection, mount→edit→save
  round-trips, ECC repair of damaged pixels, Shamir thresholds, shard loss,
  "LSB matching defeats chi-square", **a JPEG robust payload surviving a
  third-party re-encode**, and **the CTF generator's own end-to-end solve**.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean; `cargo fmt --check`
  clean; `RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings cargo doc` clean.
- **In-browser end-to-end** (Playwright, real file pickers): cover → capacity →
  embed with a hidden volume (`undetectable ✓`, PSNR 52.4 dB) → mount → open a
  file → edit → apply → protect the hidden volume → save → download.
- **In-browser album**: 3 covers → shards written while unlocked by Shamir shares
  {1,3,5} of 5 (threshold 3), then rebuilt from only **2 of the 3 pictures** using
  the *different* subset {2,4,5}.
- **In-browser Learn tab** (this round): all three lessons run, both sliders move,
  and lesson 3 reports `destroyed ✗` / `survived ✓` at every quality tried.
- **Cross-tool**: the PNG the browser produced was opened with the CLI, showing the
  edited text *and* the hidden volume still intact after a protected save.

### How to reproduce
```console
cargo test --workspace
cargo run --release -p pngfs-core --example jpeg_robustness   # the survival table
cargo run --release --example capacity -p pngfs-core          # capacity numbers
cargo run -p pngfs-cli -- ctf -o /tmp/challenge --with-solution

wasm-pack build crates/pngfs-wasm --release --target web --out-name pngfs --out-dir ../../web/pkg
python3 -m http.server -d web 8080   # open http://localhost:8080 → ▸ Learn
```

items.title: Proposal: one binary links notation shared by all implementations
items.author: konard
items.body:
## Summary

There are now two independent binary encodings of Links Notation in link-foundation, with different wire formats and no shared spec. This proposes that links-notation own a single **binary links notation** spec (and, later, encoders/decoders next to the text parser), so other projects reuse one format instead of inventing a third.

## The two existing formats

| | [links-queue](https://github.com/link-foundation/links-queue/blob/main/docs/BINARY-NOTATION-SPEC.md) (links-queue#27, PR #49) | [link-cli](https://github.com/link-foundation/link-cli/blob/issue-105-5190ec6fb31a/docs/protocol/binary-links-notation.md) (link-cli#105, PR #106) |
|---|---|---|
| Header | 11 bytes: `LNKQ` magic, version, flags, big-endian length | 1 byte: version nibble, layout, width, external-references bit (`0x10..0x1F`, never the first byte of text LiNo) |
| Link address | written per link, optional | implicit; sections with gaps leave holes |
| References | LEB128 ids, or typed inline literals (strings, integers, floats, binary, nested links) | 1/2/4/8 bytes, fixed per section; optional Hybrid external references (top bit) |
| Strings and numbers | literals | links (unary numbers, code-point lists under marker points), or external values |
| Arity | source + target, plus an optional values array | sections of any arity range (doublets, triplets, any length) |
| Golden vectors | in the spec | in the spec, checked by both the Rust and the C# test suites |
| Implementations | JS, Rust | Rust, C# (byte-identical) |

The same stores, measured with [a script](https://github.com/link-foundation/link-cli/blob/issue-105-5190ec6fb31a/docs/case-studies/issue-105/evidence/links-queue-sizes/run.sh) (bytes):

| Store | LiNo text | links-queue | link-cli store archive |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 points `(i: i i)` | 93 | 42 | 26 |
| 1000 points | 14679 | 4759 | 3500 |
| 1000 random doublets | 14104 | 6068 | 3414 |

The formats serve different needs: links-queue's is a self-describing tree of values for messages; link-cli's is address-ordered links that a doublets store can take in without a parser (`clink --export-binary` / `--import-binary` dump and restore a whole store with it, and `clink --serve` speaks it over TCP).

## Proposal

1. A spec in this repository with two layers:
   - **Packet**: sections of links, each with a gap, an arity range and a reference width; LEB128 counts; optional external references. This is link-cli's §1–§6 and could be taken over as is, including its golden vectors.
   - **Mapping** of a LiNo document onto links: link-cli's marker points (§7), with the typed literals of links-queue as a possible second mapping announced in the header.
2. Golden vectors that every implementation's tests check.
3. Encoders and decoders next to the text parsers, starting with Rust and C#, where link-cli already has implementations that could move here.

Open questions: whether a frame (magic, length, checksum, compression) belongs to the notation or to each transport; and whether the version nibble of link-cli's header byte is enough for negotiating the mapping.

Related: link-foundation/links-queue#51 (its spec and encoders disagree on self-references).

items.title: Flexibility (functionality) and maximum performance at the same time for ILinks
items.author: konard
items.body:
An solid conflict resolution example ("a win a win"):

Performance <-> Features.

It looked for me that there is only one side to this problem: either to choose perfomance way or to use features way.

So if we go performance way we should precompile as much as possible and remove all unnecessary checks while module is on operation. That means we have to create multiple implementations that are actually mostly the same (that conflicts with DRY).
And if we go features way we should create only one bloated with checks code, that is garantied to be slow because of it.

But there are solutions to both ways. We can create ILinks implementation chooser or factory, that can receive options and decide one time which implementation should be given to user. So the user does not need to remember actual implementations names. This solution have it's costs - developer time and possible a lot of "copy and paste", but actually solves performance way problem.

Than if we look at features driven way: we can also solve it. We can recompile the code of general solution for each possible options state. And then resupply the user with ILinks that contains desired implementation. Mechanism of compilation is another cost.

In both cases cost moves to reducing programmer's time, but that is ok until https://github.com/Konard/LinksPlatform/issues/105 issue is not solved.

I hope in the future there will be 3 wins at the same time: solution will be feature-rich (as expected by user), it will be the fastest possible solution (on machines of that time), and solution will be provided to user as soon as possible (as much computing power will be put to general problem solving).
